    More than any other part of the brain, the prefrontal cortex makes us
distinctly human. It gives us our personality, functions as our mind, and acts
as our personal chief executive officer. It makes it possible for you to set
goals like learning how to play poker while figuring out the steps needed to
reach them. It can evaluate your progress, recognize the implications of
your actions, and even anticipate consequences. It’s the key to your ability
to theorize, prioritize, and plan ahead. Your prefrontal cortex is the center
of your planning and decision-making circuits, the part of the brain respon-
sible for willpower, planning, goal setting, decision making, evaluating right
from wrong, and making predictions based on previous experiences.
    As you might have guessed, the prefrontal cortex is the primary deter-
minant of your personality and how you react in social situations. When it is
on point, you’ll be operating in a fashion that even your mother would be
proud of. What do you suppose happens to the prefrontal cortex when it’s
hindered by things like sleep deprivation, hunger, or alcohol? For example,
you may have experienced a prefrontal cortex “failure” when a night of
drinking led to some embarrassing drunk dialing, tweeting, or texting.
    Neuroimaging studies show that a highly developed prefrontal cortex
is necessary for you to gage your own competence, because it helps you

                        Neuropsychology and Peak Poker Performance

you must recognize your talent potential before you can develop it. It’s
also important that you are very aware of your weaknesses. Be brutally
honest with yourself. Assess what you know about them and what you
don’t. When you identify a weakness, be fanatical about learning as much
as you can to minimize it. Dunning and Kruger call this the double
whammy of incompetence. If you don’t realize that you have gaps in your
abilities, it may never occur to you to try and make improvements.
   We also rely on our prefrontal cortex to help us make sense of our
emotions. Your prefrontal cortex is where you reason about your emo-
tions, regulate their intensity, control them, and adjust to other people’s
emotions. If you were to injure your prefrontal cortex, as Phineas Gage
did, you would lose your social judgment, inhibitions, foresight, and even
logical capacities. The prefrontal cortex is an amazing piece of mental
machinery that brings together your attention, thinking, emotions, con-
science, and memories in one place.
   There are a couple of interesting points about the prefrontal cortex
that you should know. It is very slow to develop. In fact, it is the last part
of the brain to develop completely, and some parts are not fully mature
until you are 25–30 years old. This is why we do careless or more daring
things when we are young, which we would never do once we get older!
Finally, if you are having trouble getting motivated, making plans, or
thinking clearly, there’s a disconnect or snag in your prefrontal cortex,
which could be tied to an injury or, more likely, deficits in some of your
neurotransmitters. I will explain more about these soon.

Temporal lobes rest right above your ears; not surprisingly, they process
sound and music. Face and object recognition reside here, as do your
speech centers.

Your parietal lobes are found near the top of your head and deal primarily

types of recognition. Fun fact, Albert Einstein had a parietal lobe that was

Occipital Lobes
Located at the back of your brain, the occipital lobes process visual stim-
uli. If you fall down and hit the back of your head, you might see “stars”
due to your occipital lobe hitting the back of your skull.

Interior Parts of the Brain
The Brain Stem
The oldest and deepest part of your brain is called the brain stem; it’s also
known as the primitive brain. Some neuroscientists call it the reptilian
brain, because even lizards have this brain structure. It controls all of the
processes that keep you alive, like breathing, blood pressure, digestion,
and your heart beat. It sits right above your spinal cord, and also houses
the reticular activating system, which is responsible for alertness. The
primitive brain operates unconsciously, and it works 24/7 on your behalf.

The Limbic System
Right above the brain stem is your paleomammalian brain, also known as
the limbic system or emotional brain. Most of its functions involve fight-
ing, fleeing, feeding, and reproduction. The limbic system manages your
circadian rhythm (sleep–wake cycle), emotions, hunger, and sex hor-
mones. This is the area of the brain where emotions and emotional
memories are processed. While the prefrontal cortex is in charge of logic
and reason, your limbic system is tasked with handling memories and
emotions. There are several structures in this system that play an impor-
tant role in guiding our feelings. The limbic system is a critical part of your
learning, emotion, and memory systems. It contains several regions that
are especially applicable to poker players: the thalamus, the hypothala-
mus, the hippocampus, and the amygdala.

                         Figure 5: The limbic system

The Thalamus
All incoming sensory information goes to the thalamus first, and then it’s
directed to other parts of the brain for additional processing. It is also in-
volved in many cognitive activities including memory.

The Hypothalamus
Nestled just below the thalamus is your hypothalamus. It is responsible for
monitoring your internal systems in an attempt to keep everything at an
ideal level known as homeostasis. If you are feeling stressed or even a bit
depressed, your hypothalamus stays on high alert. By releasing various
hormones, it moderates your sleep, body temperature, and food and liq-
uid intake. If you are hungry, thirsty, or sleep deprived, you will not be
able to concentrate or process information effectively.
   The hypothalamus also manages stress by controlling the fight or flight
response with the release of stress hormones like cortisol and adrenaline.

Peak Poker Performance

Have you ever seen a player’s hand shake when they’re still involved in the
action? It can be the result of adrenaline; especially if they are holding a
big hand or attempting to run a monster bluff.

The Hippocampus
Your hippocampus is located near the base of the limbic area, and is re-
sponsible for consolidating learning and converting information from your
working memory into long-term memory.
   One of the most surprising discoveries in recent years is that the hip-
pocampus has the ability to produce new neurons well into old age – a
process known as neurogenesis. This is very encouraging because it
means that you can literally grow the area of your brain that helps you
learn and remember. There is also new research that shows that neuro-
genesis can be enhanced by diet and exercise as well as weakened by
sleep deprivation. Furthermore, we know that shrinkage in this area of the
brain is associated with dementia and diseases like Alzheimer’s. More
positively, there are a number of lifestyle changes you can make to en-
courage growth, which can prevent memory loss. See chapter 9.

The Amygdala
Your amygdala is attached to the end of the hippocampus, and plays an
important role in emotions like anger, rage, fear, or pleasure. It also allows
you to have memories of past, strong emotional responses. Because it is
so closely linked to the hippocampus, strong emotional events are readily
encoded into memory. The link between feelings and memories is so
strong that even recalling an intensely positive or negative experience can
generate a physical response.

Putting It All Together
Let me give an example of how the parts of the limbic system work to-
gether. Last summer, I was playing a tournament at the WSOP in the white
section of the Pavilion when all of a sudden there was a loud sound similar
to a gunshot. When that happened, my limbic system took charge in an in-

    Going back to the structures of the limbic system, here’s how the ma-
jor parts work. Your amygdala is associated with strong emotions. It also
identifies potential threats (real or imagined), and evaluates the possibility
of harm. Fear, anger, and joy all originate in this part of the brain.
    The hippocampus forms long-term memories. It’s nestled right behind
the amygdala, and they are in close communication with one another.
Whenever you experience a strong emotion, it is quickly encoded by the
hippocampus as a long-term memory. This is one reason why phobias can
develop so quickly. One exposure to a weird looking clown as a child is
enough to engender a full blown clown phobia!
    The hypothalamus regulates numerous stress hormones like adrenaline
and cortisol, and controls the fight or flight response. If you are feeling
stressed or anxious, your hypothalamus stays on high alert. Your hypo-
thalamus is likely poised at the ready if you are playing a tournament
where there’s a large amount of money on the line. Tilt is intimately asso-
ciated with the limbic system.
    Now we will go over the process that your brain uses to communicate
between all these structures.

Peak Poker Performance

Neurons
The smallest unit of your mental game system are neurons. These are the
brain cells that allow us to think, feel, move, breathe, and do everything
else that makes us human. You were born with almost your entire allot-
ment of neurons. (Although, there are a couple of spots in the brain that
continue to grow neurons up until death, most notably in the hippocam-
pus.) Neuroscientists suggest that the human brain has 100 billion neurons.
   There are over 150 types of neurons in the brain, and each individual
neuron is capable of establishing and maintaining relationships with
10,000 other neurons. It is these connections that cause your brain to
grow and change. The more connections you have, the better. Neurons
provide your computing power; they’re like billions of tiny microchips.
Their job is to transport information around your brain. Whether you are
deducing an opponent’s hand range or calculating pot-odds, your neurons
are hard at work!
   Let’s take a moment to look at how neurons connect and form circuits.
Each neuron you have is made of three parts: the soma (or cell body),
dendrites, and an axon (Figure 6). The cell body provides all of the neu-
ron’s life support.

                       Neuropsychology and Peak Poker Performance

   Dendrites are bushy and branch-like fibers that grow out of the cell
body, which receive messages in the form of electrical impulses from
other neurons. One neuron can have as many as 10,000 dendrites, which
can connect with up to 100,000 separate neurons. That’s a lot of con-
nections! If a dendrite receives a strong excitatory message from a
neighboring neuron, it will send its own electrical charge, which will pass
through the cell body. If the charge is strong enough, it will zip down the
axon, where it will pass to the next neuron’s dendrites.
   Axons are important players in your brain’s communication system, be-
cause they act on other neurons (Figure 7). Axons can range in length from
1 millimeter to about 3 feet, and some are encased in myelin. Myelinated
axons are similar to insulated electrical wires. Myelin is a fatty substance
that speeds messages along. The more you play poker, the more your
poker circuits will myelinate and the faster you’ll be able to process poker
information. Messages can travel along myelinated axons at a rate of about
220 miles per hour. Just as an aside, healthy myelin depends on a healthy
diet, because myelin is made from essential fatty acids and high-density
cholesterol. Eating foods that promote healthy myelin is critical for the
brain. It’s also important to avoid foods that degrade myelin-like saturated
fats, trans-fatty acids, and simple carbohydrates like sugar.




      Figure 7: The neuron, showing the nucleus and myelin sheath
